title: Fishing the Grand Strand: piers and charters

sections.h: Piers are the easy way in
p: You do not need a boat to fish here. The Grand Strand has several long wooden piers that reach past the surf zone, and they are as much a part of the coast as the beach itself. Apache Pier is the longest wooden fishing pier on the East Coast at about 1,206 feet. Pier 14 was rebuilt to its original length of about 1,068 feet. Second Avenue Pier, Cherry Grove Pier and Surfside Beach Pier round out the options.
Pier fishing is a good first step for families and beginners. Most piers rent rods and sell bait, and walking out on the pier without a line is also popular for sunrise and views.

Whiting and spot are the classic catch from the piers in the warmer months, and other fish show up with the seasons. Local bait shops and the people working the pier are usually the best source for what is biting this week.

Charters leave from Murrells Inlet and Little River. Salty Hooker and Fish Finder work out of Murrells Inlet, and Little River Fishing Fleet and Fine Catch Fishing Charters work out of Little River. Inshore trips are calmer and better for beginners. Offshore trips go further and take longer, so ask about trip length, what is included and whether you need a license.

list: Check South Carolina Department of Natural Resources rules on licenses, size limits and bag limits. Pier and charter rules differ.
Bring sun protection and a hat. There is not much shade on a pier.
Ask about seasickness if you are trying a charter for the first time.
Weather can cancel trips on short notice. Book with a company that tells you its rain policy up front.
